cities.name: string
rituals_and_traditions: string
cities.notes: string

cities.name: Kano
rituals_and_traditions: Community iftar in mosques and family homes
Women preparing large communal spreads for extended family
cities.notes: Hausa communities commonly serve dambu, kunu, and masa at iftar.[web:1][web:3]

cities.name: Lagos
iftar_meals: jollof rice with chicken or fish
rituals_and_traditions: Urban mosques host iftar for travelers and the poor
Strong West African jollof culture at large family gatherings
cities.notes: Jollof rice is a core celebratory dish across Nigeria and is common at Ramadan gatherings.[web:3]

cities.name: Cairo
rituals_and_traditions: Fanoos (Ramadan lanterns) decorating streets and homes
Lanterns carried by children while singing Ramadan songs
Family iftars that often extend into late-night socializing
cities.notes: Colorful fanoos lanterns and ful with karkadeh are widely associated with Egyptian Ramadan.[web:1]

cities.name: Alexandria
iftar_meals: seafood dishes alongside standard Egyptian iftar items
rituals_and_traditions: Coastal iftars with extended families
Neighborhood lantern displays similar to Cairo
cities.notes: Coastal influence adds more fish/seafood to otherwise typical Egyptian Ramadan meals.[web:1]

cities.name: Nairobi
rituals_and_traditions: Multicultural mosques with diverse cuisines at iftar
Family-focused iftars with a mix of local and South Asian dishes
cities.notes: Nairobi’s Ramadan reflects its multicultural population with both Swahili and South Asian influences.[web:6]

cities.name: Mombasa
rituals_and_traditions: Street iftar gatherings hosted by mosques and community centers
Strong Swahili coastal culture in food and dress
cities.notes: Zanzibar and Mombasa are known for public street iftars and Swahili dishes like kaimati.[web:1]

cities.name: Zanzibar City
rituals_and_traditions: Street iftar gatherings near mosques
Communal sharing of food along the seafront
cities.notes: Swahili Coast Ramadan is marked by public iftar tables and seafood-rich meals.[web:1]

cities.name: Casablanca
suhoor_meals: bread with olive oil and cheese
rituals_and_traditions: Family-centered iftar centered around harira
Traditional clothing like djellaba and kaftan for prayers and gatherings
cities.notes: Harira, rfissa, and tangia are highlighted as signature Moroccan Ramadan dishes.[web:9]

cities.name: Marrakesh
suhoor_meals: bread, olive oil, and local cheeses
iftar_meals: rfissa (chicken and lentils over shredded bread)
rituals_and_traditions: Large family gatherings after Maghrib
Old city squares buzzing at night with food stalls
cities.notes: Tanjia Marrakchia is particularly linked to Marrakesh Ramadan tables.[web:9]

cities.name: Riyadh
iftar_meals: thareed (bread soaked in lamb and vegetable stew)
kabsa (spiced rice with chicken or lamb)
rituals_and_traditions: Large family and tribal gatherings
Night prayers (taraweeh) with packed mosques
cities.notes: Thareed is a classic Saudi iftar stew, while kabsa is a national dish popular in Ramadan.[web:5][web:7]

cities.name: Jeddah
suhoor_meals: similar to Riyadh with more seafood options
rituals_and_traditions: Coastal city gatherings with extended families
Charity iftars near major mosques
cities.notes: Jeddah shares core Saudi Ramadan dishes with additional Red Sea seafood.[web:5][web:7]

cities.name: Istanbul
iftar_meals: Ramazan pidesi (special Ramadan flatbread) with meat or vegetable dishes
rituals_and_traditions: Mosques hang mahya (illuminated messages) between minarets
Public iftar tents by municipalities
Street drummers waking people for suhoor in some districts
cities.notes: Ramazan pidesi is a special bread baked only in Ramadan and widely eaten for iftar and sahur.[web:2][web:7]

cities.name: Ankara
iftar_meals: Ramazan pidesi with stews and kebabs
rituals_and_traditions: Mahya lights on major mosques
Municipal iftar programs
cities.notes: Patterns are similar nationwide with local variations in main dishes.[web:2]

cities.name: Karachi
rituals_and_traditions: Bustling iftar bazaars selling fried snacks
Charity iftar tables along main roads
Chaand raat shopping before Eid with henna and bangles
cities.notes: Iftar in Pakistan commonly features fried snacks, rose-flavored drinks, and haleem; chaand raat is a key end-of-Ramadan celebration.[web:4][web:7]

cities.name: Lahore
suhoor_meals: paratha and nihari or other meat stews
rituals_and_traditions: Old-city food streets packed after iftar
Strong communal culture around late-night eating
cities.notes: Lahore’s Ramadan is famous for its food streets and rich meaty dishes.[web:4][web:7]

cities.name: Jakarta
iftar_meals: kolak (sweet banana, coconut, palm sugar dessert)
rituals_and_traditions: Nyekar/nyadran style grave visits and prayers in some Javanese communities before Ramadan
Crowded street food markets (pasar Ramadan) each evening
cities.notes: Indonesian Ramadan includes cemetery visits (nyekar/nyadran) and abundant sweet snacks at iftar.[web:2][web:4][web:9]

cities.name: Yogyakarta
rituals_and_traditions: Padusan ritual cleansing in springs or lakes before Ramadan
Javanese cultural elements woven into pre-Ramadan observances
cities.notes: Padusan is a Javanese ritual cleansing used to welcome Ramadan.[web:2]

cities.name: Aceh
suhoor_meals: rice and fish or meat dishes
iftar_meals: meugang meat dishes (beef, goat, or buffalo) eaten around start of Ramadan
rituals_and_traditions: Meugang, a communal meat feast with family just before Ramadan begins
cities.notes: Meugang is a distinctive Acehnese pre-Ramadan meat feast.[web:2]

cities.name: Beirut
iftar_meals: rice with stews and grilled meats
rituals_and_traditions: Midfa al-iftar (iftar cannons) to signal sunset
Family and neighborhood gatherings
cities.notes: Iftar cannons are a long-standing tradition used to mark the end of each fasting day.[web:4]

cities.name: Sarajevo
rituals_and_traditions: Iftar cannon fired from Yellow Fortress to signal sunset
People gather around the fortress and mosques for iftar
cities.notes: Sarajevo maintains the iftar cannon tradition with crowds gathering at the Yellow Fortress.[web:2]

cities.name: Cape Town
desserts_and_drinks: boeber (sweet milk drink in some communities)
rituals_and_traditions: Cape Malay Muslim community hosting large family iftars
Mix of Asian and African influences in food and dress
cities.notes: Cape Malay biryani and koeksisters are iconic Cape Town Ramadan foods.[web:1]

cities.name: Dakar
suhoor_meals: thiakry (millet or couscous with yogurt and fruit)
rituals_and_traditions: Ndogou: moment of breaking fast shared communally from large bowls
Korité preparations and charity before Eid
Sufi brotherhoods (Tariqas) play a major role in religious and social life
cities.notes: Thieboudienne and café Touba are widely associated with Senegalese Ramadan; ndogou marks the communal iftar moment.

cities.name: Touba
iftar_meals: communal dishes shared at mosques and homes
rituals_and_traditions: Spiritual center of the Mouride brotherhood; pilgrimage site
Grand Magal pilgrimage draws millions; Ramadan observance is central
cities.notes: Touba is the holy city of the Mouride order; Ramadan and café Touba are central to daily life.

cities.name: Amman
iftar_meals: mansaf (lamb with rice and jameed yogurt)
rituals_and_traditions: Mansaf at large family gatherings and special Ramadan occasions
cities.notes: Mansaf, Jordan’s national dish, is central to celebrations and gatherings, including Ramadan.[web:5]

cities.name: Irbid
rituals_and_traditions: Family and tribal gatherings on weekends of Ramadan
Community support for poorer families with food parcels
cities.notes: Beyond Amman, mansaf and qatayef remain core parts of Jordanian Ramadan cuisine.[web:5]

cities.name: Dubai
suhoor_meals: khubz (Arabic bread) with cheese and dates
rituals_and_traditions: Large Ramadan tents at hotels and along the creek
Corporate and community iftars for workers and travelers
Children's Haq Al Laila style traditions of going door to door for sweets in some emirates
cities.notes: Ramadan tents and iftars with harees, thareed, machboos, and luqaimat are common throughout the UAE.[web:4][web:12][web:18]

cities.name: Abu Dhabi
suhoor_meals: similar to Dubai with emphasis on bread, cheese, dates
rituals_and_traditions: Government-organized charity iftars
Family-focused evenings with taraweeh in major mosques
cities.notes: Abu Dhabi follows broader Gulf food patterns with strong emphasis on hospitality and charity.[web:4][web:12]

cities.name: Doha
rituals_and_traditions: Gargee'an around mid-Ramadan where children dress up and collect sweets
Ramadan tents in hotels and majlis-style gatherings
cities.notes: Gargee'an is celebrated mid-Ramadan in parts of the Gulf, including Qatar, with children collecting sweets.[web:18]

cities.name: Kuwait City
rituals_and_traditions: Gargee'an on the 15th of Ramadan with children receiving sweets from neighbors
Family majlis gatherings late into the night
cities.notes: Kuwait shares Gargee'an traditions with other Gulf states along with typical Gulf Ramadan dishes.[web:18]

cities.name: Manama
rituals_and_traditions: Gargee'an celebrations around mid-Ramadan
Community iftars supported by charities and mosques
cities.notes: Bahrain's mid-Ramadan children's celebrations mirror Gargee'an traditions seen elsewhere in the Gulf.[web:18]

cities.name: Muscat
rituals_and_traditions: Strong emphasis on neighborhood sharing and charity
Families gathering with traditional Omani halwa after iftar
cities.notes: Core Gulf dishes like harees and thareed appear alongside local Omani halwa in Ramadan.[web:5][web:7]

cities.name: Tehran
suhoor_meals: barbari bread with cheese and herbs
rituals_and_traditions: Late-night street life after iftar
Special religious gatherings and Quran recitation sessions
cities.notes: Ash-e reshteh and sholeh zard are widely associated with Iranian Ramadan tables.[web:12][web:13]

cities.name: Mazandaran (province)
rituals_and_traditions: Some communities begin fasting three days before Ramadan starts, effectively fasting 33 days
cities.notes: In Mazandaran, some people traditionally start fasting at the end of Sha'ban, adding three extra days.[web:12]

cities.name: Hyderabad
rituals_and_traditions: Haleem stalls all over the city during Ramadan
Night markets around Charminar packed after taraweeh
cities.notes: Hyderabadi haleem is one of the most famous South Asian Ramadan dishes.[web:5][web:13]

cities.name: Delhi
rituals_and_traditions: Old Delhi food streets like Jama Masjid area crowded for iftar and late-night snacks
Seheriwalas (drummers) waking people up for suhoor in some neighborhoods
cities.notes: India shares many Ramadan foods with Pakistan and Bangladesh, including haleem, biryani, and rooh afza drinks.[web:5][web:13][web:16]

cities.name: Kolkata
rituals_and_traditions: Ramadan food lanes around Zakaria Street and central mosques
Strong street-food culture after iftar
cities.notes: Kolkata's Ramadan is known for dense street-food scenes centered on mosques and market lanes.[web:4]

cities.name: Dhaka
iftar_meals: panta ilish (fermented rice with hilsa fish) for some
rituals_and_traditions: Crowded iftar markets selling fritters and biryanis
Strong culture of giving food to the poor during Ramadan
cities.notes: Bangladeshi iftars feature biryani, panta ilish, and various fried snacks, with a big emphasis on charity.[web:4][web:14]

cities.name: Kuala Lumpur
rituals_and_traditions: Bazaar Ramadan markets selling a wide variety of take-away iftar foods
Family-centric iftars that blend Malay, Chinese, and Indian culinary influences
cities.notes: Bazaar Ramadan is a defining Malaysian institution, with temporary markets dedicated to iftar food.[web:14]

cities.name: Penang
rituals_and_traditions: Heritage streets lined with Ramadan food stalls
Mix of Malay and Indian Muslim influences
cities.notes: Penang's Ramadan food reflects its reputation as a food capital with strong Indian Muslim presence.[web:14]

cities.name: Tunis
rituals_and_traditions: Iftar cannon firing in some areas
Family gatherings around hearty soups and pastries
cities.notes: Lablabi and brik are emblematic Tunisian Ramadan dishes.[web:14]

cities.name: Tashkent
rituals_and_traditions: Community iftars with extended family and neighbors
Evening prayers followed by tea and sweets
cities.notes: Plov, shashlik, and samsa are common Uzbek dishes served during Ramadan.[web:14]

cities.name: Almaty
rituals_and_traditions: Strong emphasis on family gatherings at iftar
Taraweeh prayers at neighborhood mosques
cities.notes: Plov and beshbarmak appear in Kazakh Ramadan meals along with shared family iftars.[web:14]

cities.name: Sanaa
rituals_and_traditions: Extended family meals with shared platters
Coffee and qat sessions in some communities after taraweeh
cities.notes: Aseeda is a well-known Yemeni Ramadan dish, often eaten with broth by hand.[web:13]
